newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks rebound seen after recent drastic dive.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks rebound seen after recent drastic dive.

text.p: Battered Thai stocks, now at more than three-year-lows, could slide further in the near term, stock analysts said on Tuesday.
But they did not rule out a rebound soon because recent steep falls were too drastic.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index has plummeted 14.05 percent or 154.38 points over the past five trading days.

The bourse fell 60.26 points on Monday as foreign funds sold off bank stocks on fears their profitability might be hurt by new central bank limits on importing foreign loans. It was seen by analysts as one of the heaviest in the Thai bourse's history.

"The market ought to rebound later this week as selling, mainly by foreigners, will probably slow down and because stocks have been oversold already," analyst Dusanee Klewpatinontha of Nithipat Capital told Reuters.
The index closed on Monday at 944.63 points, its lowest level since August 1993. Analysts said they believed strong support existed around the 900-level.

Investors fear the growth in bank profits may fall to single digits from 15.6 percent in 1995, analysts said. Investors were worried that bank profits may suffer because interest rates were now seen unlikely to fall by year's end as had been expected earlier.
Bangkok Bank Plc, Thailand's top bank, said it planned to raise rates on fixed deposits by about 25 basis points to halt the falling market share of deposits.
"The average profit growth to be earned by banks this year would be around nine percent," said analyst Virat Tippanontakul of First Asia Securities.

Another analyst, who requested anonymity, said the fall may have been compounded by some Thai politicians who were selling heavily on the market to generate proceeds for use in campaigns ahead of the November 17 polls.
"Money talks in Thai politics. Some politicians who have companies listed on the bourse are selling stocks, too, in order to get cash for this election," the analyst said.

Foreign investors, who mainly hold bank and finance counters, have been selling on fears over the slowing Thai economy, which has been beset by a widening current account deficit and sagging exports growth.
Weak Thai exports were expected to keep the 1996 current account deficit at the 1995 level of 8.1 percent of gross domestic product. The Bank of Thailand had projected a reduced 7.8 percent deficit.
Given the current weak Thai economy, investors were worried that third-quarter and even fourth-quarter corporate profits might be worse than expected, analysts said.

An analyst at HG Asia said: "Many investors are worried about the asset quality of banks and of non-performing loans. The concern is understandable, but I must say the heavy selling seen was a bit exaggerated."

As the index kept sliding, a broker from Dhana Siam Finance and Securities said some foreign funds could start returning since some bank and finance company share prices were becoming quite attractive.
"There is talk that some funds feel the market has been oversold and will start bargain hunting soon," he said.
